faq.a: Vasodilation from progesterone and placental hormones reduces systemic vascular resistance, lowering systolic and diastolic pressures.
faq.q: Why does blood pressure often fall in early pregnancy?

faq.a: Mild proteinuria (≤ 1+) is common due to increased GFR; ≥ 2+ or persistent proteinuria with hypertension suggests pre‑eclampsia.
faq.q: Is proteinuria always abnormal in pregnancy?

faq.a: Malaria causes hemolysis and anemia, reducing oxygen‑carrying capacity; combined with increased maternal demand, it can precipitate fetal growth restriction and maternal cardiac strain.
faq.q: How does malaria affect pregnancy physiology?

exam: A 28‑year‑old at 30 weeks presents with BP 150/95 mmHg, 2+ proteinuria, and mild oedema — what is the next step and why? — Diagnose pre‑eclampsia; initiate antihypertensive (e.g., labetalol) and magnesium sulfate, arrange delivery planning.

A woman with known rheumatic mitral stenosis becomes pregnant; her heart rate is 115 bpm and she has new crackles — how does normal pregnancy physiology exacerbate her condition and what immediate measures are indicated? — Increased plasma volume and cardiac output overload stenotic valve; give diuretics, beta‑blocker, and consider early delivery.

In a malaria‑endemic area, a pregnant woman has haemoglobin 7 g/dL; what physiological changes are compromised and what management priorities arise? — Reduced oxygen delivery despite ↑ cardiac output; give antimalarial therapy, blood transfusion if needed, and monitor for cardiac decompensation.

Why does the PaCO₂ fall during pregnancy and how does this affect the interpretation of arterial blood gases? — Progesterone stimulates ventilation; normal pregnancy ABG shows PaCO₂ 30‑32 mmHg, so a value of 35 mmHg may indicate hypoventilation.

A patient in labour has a sudden drop in systolic BP to 80 mmHg without bleeding — what physiological cause should be considered and what is the immediate action? — Possible supine aortocaval compression; reposition to left lateral tilt and give IV fluids.

How would you differentiate physiologic dyspnoea of pregnancy from early heart failure in a low‑resource setting? — Physiologic dyspnoea improves with rest and lacks peripheral oedema; heart failure shows persistent tachycardia, basilar crackles, and worsening oedema; use bedside exam and simple chest auscultation.

Explain the role of placental lactogen in maternal glucose metabolism and its clinical relevance. — Increases insulin resistance to spare glucose for the fetus; may unmask gestational diabetes, requiring OGTT screening at 24‑28 weeks.

A woman at 22 weeks reports excessive thirst and polyuria; urine dipstick is negative for glucose — what physiological change explains this and when should you be concerned? — Pregnancy‑induced osmotic diuresis from increased plasma volume; concern if accompanied by hyperglycaemia or dehydration.
ai.title: Physiology of Normal Pregnancy
ai.subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
ai.summary: Pregnancy triggers coordinated cardiovascular, respiratory, renal and endocrine changes to support the fetus. Understanding these adaptations helps clinicians recognise abnormal patterns and manage complications in low‑resource settings.

b: Progesterone drives respiratory drive and smooth‑muscle relaxation
sections.p: Normal pregnancy is a state of increased metabolic demand and altered organ function. Changes begin early and intensify by the third trimester, preparing the mother for fetal growth and delivery.

b: Uterine arterial remodeling reduces uteroplacental resistance
Renal plasma flow ↑ 80 % → GFR ↑ 50 % → physiologic proteinuria
Progesterone ↑ ventilation → PaCO₂ falls 4‑5 mmHg, causing mild respiratory alkalosis
sections.p: Hormonal signals (hCG, progesterone, estrogen) remodel the uterus, placenta and maternal vasculature. The placenta acts as an endocrine organ, producing hormones that sustain the pregnancy and modulate maternal physiology.

b: Renin‑angiotensin‑aldosterone system activated by expanded volume but offset by vasodilation
Placental lactogen antagonises insulin → mild gestational insulin resistance
Thyroid hormone production rises 30‑50 % to meet increased metabolic demand
sections.p: Feedback loops involving the placenta, maternal kidneys and endocrine glands maintain homeostasis. In low‑resource settings, malnutrition or infection can blunt these mechanisms.

b: Inadequate plasma volume expansion → early-onset pre‑eclampsia
Excessive cardiac output with underlying heart disease → heart failure
Severe anemia or malaria → impaired oxygen delivery, fetal growth restriction
sections.p: Failure of normal adaptation leads to obstetric complications. Recognise patterns that suggest pathology and prioritize urgent investigations.

b: Blood pressure trend: rise > 140/90 mmHg after 20 weeks suggests pre‑eclampsia
Fundal height lagging > 2 cm behind gestational age signals growth restriction
Persistent tachycardia > 110 bpm with dyspnoea may indicate cardiac overload
sections.p: Bedside assessment integrates history, vitals and simple tests. In low‑resource hospitals, clinicians rely on clinical signs and point‑of‑care tools.

t.b: Is hypertension present? → Diagnosis of gestational hypertension or pre‑eclampsia; if unavailable, use manual sphygmomanometer
Detects ≥ 1+ protein → supports pre‑eclampsia; if dipstick unavailable, assess for oedema and visual changes
Assesses fetal growth; discrepancy > 2 cm prompts ultrasound if available, otherwise consider maternal anemia, infection, or malnutrition

b: Explain why cardiac output peaks in the second trimester and falls in the third
Link physiologic proteinuria to increased GFR, and differentiate from pathological proteinuria
Discuss how malaria‑induced anaemia worsens maternal oxygen delivery despite increased cardiac output
sections.p: Examiners test integration of physiology with clinical decision‑making. Focus on why each sign matters and how it guides management.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe headache, visual disturbances, or epigastric pain with hypertension → possible eclampsia
Rapidly rising dyspnoea, chest pain, or peripheral oedema in a woman with known heart disease → acute heart failure
Fever > 38 °C with chills in any trimester, especially with malaria endemicity → severe infection
